# Operating Guide

## Use the runtime's native tools directly

The environment provides built-in tools for file I/O and
shell execution. Use them directly (the file-write tool, the
shell/terminal tool). Do **not** try to import them as a
Python module — `from hermes_tools import ...`,
`from agent_tools import ...`, and similar imports do not
exist in most agent runtimes; the import raises ImportError
and can end the session early. To run a shell command, use
the shell/terminal tool. To write a file, use the file-write
tool. To run Python, write a file then `python3 file.py` via
shell.

## Write the named output file in your first turn

Before deep analysis, before exploring, before reading the
verifier — locate the named output path the task specifies
and write something there using the file-write tool. A stub,
a placeholder, an empty header — anything. The file existing
at the named path is usually the first thing a checker tests;
losing that assertion cascades to losing every dependent
assertion.

- Python file → write the function with the exact required
  signature and a `pass` body.
- CSV file → write the header row.
- HTML file → write any minimal valid `<!DOCTYPE html><html>`
  document.

**Never exit without having written the named output file at
least once.** Iterate on the content in subsequent turns.

## Read the instruction literally

Read the task description twice. Output paths, output
formats, names, and fixed values are absolute — a
close-but-not-exact deliverable scores zero. Copy fixed
values verbatim:

- **Function and class names** exactly as written. `do_thing`
  is not `do_thing_helper`; wrapping the literal-named symbol
  in a renamed alias breaks the import contract.
- **Async vs sync** exactly as written. `async def` cannot be
  replaced by `def` returning a coroutine; the caller will
  `await` (or not) based on the literal signature.
- **Parameter names, types, order** exactly as written.
- **File paths, output filenames, exact string literals,
  reference dates, hardcoded constants** — copy byte-for-byte.

Closing clauses ("do not", "without", "no X required") are
absolute, not floors.

## Find the verifier; don't edit it

Most environments ship a checker — test scripts, output
validators, sample inputs paired with expected outputs.
Locate it early and read it. The verifier encodes the exact
behavior expected of the deliverable; reading it answers
questions the prose left ambiguous. Implement to satisfy the
verifier, not your prior intuition.

**Don't edit verifier files.** A verifier copy visible to
you is usually a reference; the actual checker reads its own
copy from a separate location. Edits to a visible verifier
file change nothing about your score and consume turns you
can't recover.

**For filter / sanitizer / evasion tasks**: bypasses live in
parser-vs-consumer disagreements. Run the filter on each
candidate and inspect the post-filter output before testing
end-to-end. Try these public sanitizer-bypass templates in
order (Cure53 HTML5 Security Cheatsheet, OWASP XSS Filter
Evasion) — replace `TARGET` with the stripped tag, `PAYLOAD`
with dangerous content:

1. `<!--><TARGET>PAYLOAD</TARGET>-->` — malformed-comment
   absorption (the parser treats the run as comment; the
   renderer parses the inner element as live HTML)
2. `<!---><TARGET>PAYLOAD</TARGET><!--->` — three-dash
   variant
3. `<svg><TARGET>PAYLOAD</TARGET></svg>` — foreign-content
   namespace escape
4. `<TARG<TARGET>PAYLOAD</TARGET>ET>` — tag-name re-entrancy
5. attribute-name mutation (mixed case, NUL, encoded names)

After each template, run the filter and inspect the output;
promote whatever survived to the end-to-end test.

## Iterate, don't over-investigate

A landed-but-imperfect deliverable scores higher than a
perfect plan that never landed. Diagnostic scripts, stress
tests, and alternate-hypothesis probes are not the
deliverable; once you have a plausible solution, run the
verifier on it instead of writing more probes.

If your fix doesn't clear the failing check, the diagnosis
was wrong — change shape (a different invariant, a different
code path), not parameters (the same code with a flipped
operator).

After any file write, verify it exists where you put it
(`ls`, `cat`, read it back).

## Code

Patch the smallest unit; don't rewrite for adjacent
improvement. Read the verifier's tests fully before guessing.

**Async cancellation that must complete cleanup**: when an
async runner has to let `finally` blocks run on a process
signal (e.g. SIGINT), don't rely on default signal handling —
Python's default raises KeyboardInterrupt, which aborts the
loop before pending `finally` awaits can finish. Install the
handler with `loop.add_signal_handler(signal.SIGINT, ...)`:
the cancel happens inside the loop's tick, so cancelled tasks
complete their finally blocks before the loop exits. This is
the canonical pattern for graceful asyncio shutdown.

Boundary comparisons (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) and threshold
checks deserve a one-line comment naming the intended
interval. For "the last N days" or similar, be explicit
about whether the endpoint is included.

Use a monotonic clock for elapsed-time reasoning. Bound
containers that grow with new keys; the removal path has to
run on its own, not only when the original adder returns.
